extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, patent practitioners (attorneys/agents), and IP litigators
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on applying U.S. patent obviousness law (KSR/Graham framework) in examination and disputes, including how to treat prior art, PHOSITA perspective, motivation to combine, and evidentiary requirements for rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Graham Factors (four-factor analysis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The objective four-factor analysis announced in Graham v. John Deere: (1) the scope and content of the prior art; (2) the differences between the prior art and the claims at issue; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the pertinent art; and (4) secondary considerations (commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, failure of others, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: KSR followed this Graham framework; the guidance emphasizes applying these factors (and considering them together) when determining obviousness. The office reiterates that the Graham factors remain central to the analysis. Example citations: KSR, 550 U.S. at 406 (quoting Graham).

rubrics_metrics.name: PHOSITA perspective (ordinary creativity and common sense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art and claimed inventions must be viewed through the perspective of a person having ordinary skill in the art (PHOSITA), who is considered to have ordinary creativity and common sense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The USPTO guidance and Federal Circuit decisions repeatedly stress viewing prior art from a PHOSITA's perspective. This perspective can explain why an ordinarily skilled artisan would be motivated to combine or modify references. MPEP 2141 instructs examiners to consider a PHOSITA's 'ordinary creativity.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of prior art includes reasonable suggestions (not just explicit teachings)
rubrics_metrics.description: The scope of prior art must be understood to include not just explicit teachings, but also what the art reasonably suggests to a PHOSITA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per KSR, the hypothetical PHOSITA's understanding and what the art 'reasonably suggests' are part of the scope. Examiners should not limit prior art to only express disclosures; consider reasonable inferences a PHOSITA would draw. This is part of the 'flexibility' KSR requires in determining prior art scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous art determination
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art is analogous when it shares the 'same field of endeavor' with, and is 'reasonably pertinent' to, the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination of whether a reference is analogous art should take into account relevant evidence in the record cited by parties to demonstrate the knowledge and perspective of a PHOSITA (citing Airbus S.A.S. v. Firepass). Examine whether the reference would have been within the ordinary knowledge or concern of a PHOSITA such that it is reasonably pertinent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivation to combine references
rubrics_metrics.description: A key concept: a PHOSITA must be motivated to combine multiple prior art references (or to modify a reference) to arrive at the claimed invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation can be explicit in references or supported by evidence of the skilled artisan's knowledge and perspective. Examples of reasons include market forces, known needs or problems in the field, and the general desire of a PHOSITA to improve on the prior art (citing Plantronics v. Aliph, In re Ethicon, Intel v. Qualcomm). The Federal Circuit treats motivation flexibly; any motivation supported by evidence may suffice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for articulated reasoning and evidentiary support for rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: Any legally proper obviousness rejection must 'identify facts and then articulate sound reasoning that leads to the conclusion that the claims would have been obvious to a PHOSITA.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP 2142 and the USPTO guidance require clear articulation of the reasons why the claimed invention would have been obvious; examiners must provide adequate analysis based on evidentiary support. A mere conclusory statement without fact-based reasoning is insufficient. The guidance calls out the need for this as a frequent theme in post-KSR cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective indicia / secondary considerations must be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Secondary considerations (objective indicia) such as commercial success, long-felt but unsolved needs, and failure of others must be considered as part of the whole obviousness analysis, not as an afterthought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit precedent emphasizes that consideration of objective indicia is part of the whole analysis (citing Leo Pharmaceutical Products v. Rea). Examiners and decisionmakers should weigh these factors with evidentiary support and integrate them into the overall obviousness determination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in application but with limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The KSR approach requires flexibility in applying Graham factors and determining obviousness, but that flexibility has limits and does not negate the need for articulated reasoning and evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The guidance cautions against rigid rules that prevent factfinders from using common sense, yet stresses that flexibility 'is not without its limits'—examiners cannot dispense with factual support or reasoned analysis. Commentators worry that emphasizing flexibility could result in more obviousness rejections; the guidance attempts to curb overreach by requiring evidence and articulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to follow Federal Circuit precedent and MPEP instruction
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent examiners are required to apply the law of obviousness consistent with Federal Circuit precedent and the MPEP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes MPEP instructions (e.g., MPEP 2141 and subsections) that inform examiners how to treat prior art and PHOSITA perspective. Examiners must reconcile USPTO practice with controlling Federal Circuit decisions and ensure rejections comport with both precedent and MPEP guidance.
